annotations.text:
Where should the app's notifications live?

The ask: notices inside the dock don't feel right — maybe above it, or somewhere else. And maybe the AI's notices and the toast's actions should be combined.

Five directions, drawn against the real desktop tokens (406px sidebar, the well/pill ramp, the elev shadow family) rather than a generic mockup — so what you're judging is what it would actually look like.

Start at the Reference board for what speaks today and why the two systems overlap.

Nothing here is built. Pick a direction — or parts of several — and it becomes the ticket.

Reference — the two systems, as they are

Four notices can occupy the dock stack, ranked by what they ask of you rather than by which feature raised them. Eighteen action families raise an undo toast. Both anchor to the bottom of the sidebar, 8px apart.

The overlap at the foot of the board is the thing worth looking at: a receipt notice and an undo toast are the same sentence wearing different chrome.

A — Today (baseline)

What ships now: the stack sits inside the dock capsule above the user row; the undo toast floats exactly 8px above that same capsule.

The case for it, and it is a real one: one edge of the screen where you and the app talk. That was the argument that moved notices out of the canvas, a modal and a toast in the first place.

The tradeoff — and this is the complaint: every notice that arrives or leaves changes the capsule's height, so the omnibar, the one control you aim at without looking, moves under your cursor. The stack also competes with the Braindump for the same column, which is why it is capped at two rows.

B — Detached shelf

The stack lifts out of the capsule into its own card in the gap above the dock. The dock returns to a fixed height.

Why: it is the smallest move that fixes the actual defect — the omnibar stops moving — and it is what "maybe above the dock" literally asks for. The shelf can now grow past two rows without the capture bar caring, so the cap becomes a choice instead of rent.

Tradeoff: three stacked surfaces at the foot of the sidebar (toast, shelf, dock), each with its own border and shadow. It fixes the movement but not the duplication — a receipt and a toast are still drawn twice, 8px apart.

C — One signal stack (the combination you floated)

Toasts and notices become the same row in one surface. A transient row carries an expiry hairline and falls into a scrollback rather than vanishing; a persistent one simply stays until answered.

Why: "Moved 3 overdue · Undo" and "Completed: Morning pages · Undo" are the same sentence, so stop drawing them twice. It also gives undo a history, which a five-second toast never had — miss it and the action is currently unrecoverable from the UI.

Tradeoff: the most work of the five, and it argues with the dock's own membership rule that a line is earned by a pending decision. Receipts would now live there by default. This is the direction most at risk of silting into a notification centre nobody reads — the exact failure the current design was written to avoid.

D — Canvas header inbox

Notices leave the sidebar entirely for a counted glyph in the canvas header, opening a panel. The dock becomes pure capture.

Why: it is the pattern every user already knows, it scales to any number of notices without a cap, and it cleanly separates "you speak" (sidebar) from "the app speaks" (canvas).

Tradeoff: this is the one the code comments argue against by name — a badge you learn to ignore. A count is not a decision, and a bell defers every notice equally, including the one that says the app could not reach your items. If you like this shape, the honest version keeps blocked-rank notices out of it.

E — Back to the object

Each notice returns to the thing it is about: the sweep receipt sits on the day whose contents it changed, end-of-day at the foot of the evening bucket. The dock keeps at most one line — the highest-ranked question with nowhere else to live.

Why: the most Anchor-shaped answer, and the only one that reduces total surface instead of relocating it. A notice standing next to the thing it changed needs no words to say what it is about, which is also how the pause state and the day's suppression line already work.

Tradeoff: a notice you never scroll to is a notice you never see, so anything genuinely urgent still needs the dock line — and deciding which is which is a judgement per notice rather than a rule the code can enforce.
